alt: Nine disciplines a school may teach, from integrated humanities and history to psychology and world religions, narrow to only three on-screen eAssessment subjects: history, geography and integrated humanities.
caption: Whatever discipline is taught, the eAssessment comes in only three subjects.

alt: A bar split by marks: investigating 26, communicating 18 and thinking critically 36, out of 80. Investigating uses criteria A and B; communicating A and C; thinking critically, the largest task, A, C and D and ends in extended writing.
caption: Thinking critically carries 36 of the 80 marks and ends in extended writing.

alt: Summarising a source extracts its facts; evaluating it says what it can and cannot tell you for a research purpose. Official sample questions test this on one source, a value or limitation of source B, and comparatively, the usefulness of sources C and D for studying protest movements.
caption: Evaluate usefulness for a purpose, on one source or two; do not just summarise.

alt: A sample to-what-extent question about protest movements leads to three steps: take a position, weigh it against alternatives, and reach a reasoned judgement. A narrative description cannot reach top marks; a structured argument can.
caption: Take a position, weigh alternatives and judge: description alone cannot reach the top.

alt: Ten topic tiles from the official brief, including demographics and human movements, settlement and urban morphology, warfare and peacekeeping, rights and social protest, trade, aid and exchange, and industrialization and technological developments.
caption: The listed topics cross disciplines, so expect overlap whatever you were taught.
